question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf f(u)=\begin{bmatrix}\cos{\left(u \right)} \\ 3 \\ 4 - u^{2}\end{bmatrix}$ and $u(t)=4 t^{3}$. Find $(\mathbf f\circ u)'(t)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate the outer function component by component and the scalar inner function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf f'(u) & =\begin{bmatrix}- \sin{\left(u \right)} \\ 0 \\ - 2 u\end{bmatrix} \\ u'(t) & =12 t^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the inner input and multiply **every component** by the same scalar derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf f\circ u)'(t) & =\mathbf f'(u(t))u'(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}- \sin{\left(4 t^{3} \right)} \\ 0 \\ - 8 t^{3}\end{bmatrix}\cdot\left(12 t^{2}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}- 12 t^{2} \sin{\left(4 t^{3} \right)} \\ 0 \\ - 96 t^{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}$ given that $f(t)=⟨t^{3},\,t,\,\ln{(t )}⟩$ and $v(t)=t.$ Assume $t>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar function multiple rule:

$$
(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}=v(t)f^{\prime}(t)+v^{\prime}(t)f(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{3})=3 t^{2} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\ln{(t )})=\frac{1}{t} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =⟨3 t^{2},\,1,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ v^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(t)⟨3 t^{2},\,1,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨3 t^{3},\,t,\,1⟩ \\ P_2 & =(1)⟨t^{3},\,t,\,\ln{(t )}⟩ \\  & =⟨t^{3},\,t,\,\ln{(t )}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(v(t)f(t))^{\prime} & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =⟨4 t^{3},\,2 t,\,\ln{(t )} + 1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}$ given that $f(t)=⟨e^{t + 3},\,e^{- t},\,e^{3 t}⟩$ and $v(t)=e^{t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar function multiple rule:

$$
(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}=v(t)f^{\prime}(t)+v^{\prime}(t)f(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{t + 3})=e^{t + 3} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{- t})=- e^{- t} \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{3 t})=3 e^{3 t} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =⟨e^{t + 3},\,- e^{- t},\,3 e^{3 t}⟩ \\ v^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{t})=e^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(e^{t})⟨e^{t + 3},\,- e^{- t},\,3 e^{3 t}⟩ \\  & =⟨e^{t} e^{t + 3},\,-1,\,3 e^{4 t}⟩ \\ P_2 & =(e^{t})⟨e^{t + 3},\,e^{- t},\,e^{3 t}⟩ \\  & =⟨e^{t} e^{t + 3},\,1,\,e^{4 t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(v(t)f(t))^{\prime} & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =⟨2 e^{2 t + 3},\,0,\,4 e^{4 t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{5^{t}}{25}\right)=\frac{5^{t} \ln{(5 )}}{25} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(5^{2 t} - 3)=2 \cdot 5^{2 t} \ln{(5 )} \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(5^{t})=5^{t} \ln{(5 )} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5^{t} \ln{(5 )}}{25} \\ 2 \cdot 5^{2 t} \ln{(5 )} \\ 5^{t} \ln{(5 )}\end{bmatrix} \\ v^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(5^{- t})=- 5^{- t} \ln{(5 )}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(5^{- t})\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5^{t} \ln{(5 )}}{25} \\ 2 \cdot 5^{2 t} \ln{(5 )} \\ 5^{t} \ln{(5 )}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\ln{(5 )}}{25} \\ 2 \cdot 5^{t} \ln{(5 )} \\ \ln{(5 )}\end{bmatrix} \\ P_2 & =(- 5^{- t} \ln{(5 )})\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5^{t}}{25} \\ 5^{2 t} - 3 \\ 5^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}- \frac{\ln{(5 )}}{25} \\ - 5^{t} \ln{(5 )} + 3 \cdot 5^{- t} \ln{(5 )} \\ - \ln{(5 )}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Find $(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t)$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =(2 t + 3)\,i- 3 t\,j- 2 t\,k \\ g(t) & =(t^{2} + t)\,i+t^{3}\,j+t\,k\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the dot product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime}(t)\cdot g(t)+f(t)\cdot g^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t + 3)=2 \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t)=-3 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 2 t)=-2 \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =2\,i-3\,j-2\,k \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{2} + t)=2 t + 1 \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{3})=3 t^{2} \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1 \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =(2 t + 1)\,i+3 t^{2}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(2)(t^{2} + t)+(-3)(t^{3})+(-2)(t) \\  & =- 3 t^{3} + 2 t^{2} \\ P_2 & =(2 t + 3)(2 t + 1)+(- 3 t)(3 t^{2})+(- 2 t)(1) \\  & =- 9 t^{3} + 4 t^{2} + 6 t + 3\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =- 12 t^{3} + 6 t^{2} + 6 t + 3\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)=- \frac{2}{t^{2}} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\ln{(t )})=\frac{1}{t} \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t)=-3 \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =- \frac{2}{t^{2}}\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j-3\,k \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)=- \frac{1}{t^{2}} \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t)=-3 \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 \ln{(t )})=\frac{3}{t} \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\,i-3\,j+\frac{3}{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\left(- \frac{2}{t^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)(- 3 t)+(-3)(3 \ln{(t )}) \\  & =- 9 \ln{(t )} - 3 - \frac{2}{t^{3}} \\ P_2 & =\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)\left(- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)+(\ln{(t )})(-3)+(- 3 t)\left(\frac{3}{t}\right) \\  & =- 3 \ln{(t )} - 9 - \frac{2}{t^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =- 12 \ln{(t )} - 12 - \frac{4}{t^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given $f(t)=(2 - t^{2})\,i+3 t\,j+t^{3}\,k$, find $(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the dot product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime\prime}(t)\cdot f(t)+f^{\prime}(t)\cdot f^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 - t^{2})=- 2 t \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t)=3 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{3})=3 t^{2} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =- 2 t\,i+3\,j+3 t^{2}\,k \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 2 t)=-2 \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3)=0 \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t^{2})=6 t \\ f^{\prime\prime}(t) & =-2\,i+6 t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(-2)(2 - t^{2})+(0)(3 t)+(6 t)(t^{3}) \\  & =6 t^{4} + 2 t^{2} - 4 \\ P_2 & =(- 2 t)(- 2 t)+(3)(3)+(3 t^{2})(3 t^{2}) \\  & =9 t^{4} + 4 t^{2} + 9\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =15 t^{4} + 6 t^{2} + 5\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find $(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}t^{2} \\ -3 \\ t + 3\end{bmatrix} \\ g(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}t - 1 \\ - 3 t \\ - t^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cross product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times g^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{2})=2 t \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(-3)=0 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t + 3)=1 \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 t \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t - 1)=1 \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t)=-3 \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- t^{2})=- 2 t \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3 \\ - 2 t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 t & 0 & 1 \\ t - 1 & - 3 t & - t^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{1,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ - 3 t & - t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=3 t \\ P_{1,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}2 t & 1 \\ t - 1 & - t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=2 t^{3} + t - 1 \\ P_{1,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 t & 0 \\ t - 1 & - 3 t\end{vmatrix}=- 6 t^{2} \\ P_1 & =\begin{bmatrix}3 t \\ 2 t^{3} + t - 1 \\ - 6 t^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ P_2 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ t^{2} & -3 & t + 3 \\ 1 & -3 & - 2 t\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{2,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & t + 3 \\ -3 & - 2 t\end{vmatrix}=9 t + 9 \\ P_{2,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}t^{2} & t + 3 \\ 1 & - 2 t\end{vmatrix}=2 t^{3} + t + 3 \\ P_{2,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}t^{2} & -3 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix}=3 - 3 t^{2} \\ P_2 & =\begin{bmatrix}9 t + 9 \\ 2 t^{3} + t + 3 \\ 3 - 3 t^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\times g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 t + 9 \\ 4 t^{3} + 2 t + 2 \\ 3 - 9 t^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find $(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨3,\,- 2 t,\,- 3 t^{2}⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨3 - 3 t,\,3 t^{2},\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cross product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times g^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3)=0 \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 2 t)=-2 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t^{2})=- 6 t \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =⟨0,\,-2,\,- 6 t⟩ \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 - 3 t)=-3 \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t^{2})=6 t \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2)=0 \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =⟨-3,\,6 t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & -2 & - 6 t \\ 3 - 3 t & 3 t^{2} & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{1,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & - 6 t \\ 3 t^{2} & 2\end{vmatrix}=18 t^{3} - 4 \\ P_{1,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}0 & - 6 t \\ 3 - 3 t & 2\end{vmatrix}=18 t^{2} - 18 t \\ P_{1,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 3 - 3 t & 3 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=6 - 6 t \\ P_1 & =⟨18 t^{3} - 4,\,18 t^{2} - 18 t,\,6 - 6 t⟩ \\ P_2 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 3 & - 2 t & - 3 t^{2} \\ -3 & 6 t & 0\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{2,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}- 2 t & - 3 t^{2} \\ 6 t & 0\end{vmatrix}=18 t^{3} \\ P_{2,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}3 & - 3 t^{2} \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix}=9 t^{2} \\ P_{2,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & - 2 t \\ -3 & 6 t\end{vmatrix}=12 t \\ P_2 & =⟨18 t^{3},\,9 t^{2},\,12 t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\times g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =⟨36 t^{3} - 4,\,27 t^{2} - 18 t,\,6 t + 6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

(f^{\prime}\times f)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime\prime}(t)\times f(t)+f^{\prime}(t)\times f^{\prime}(t)

$$

$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 18 t & -4 & 0 \\ 3 t^{3} - 3 & 1 - 2 t^{2} & 1 - 3 t\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{1,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}-4 & 0 \\ 1 - 2 t^{2} & 1 - 3 t\end{vmatrix}=12 t - 4 \\ P_{1,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}18 t & 0 \\ 3 t^{3} - 3 & 1 - 3 t\end{vmatrix}=54 t^{2} - 18 t \\ P_{1,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}18 t & -4 \\ 3 t^{3} - 3 & 1 - 2 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=- 24 t^{3} + 18 t - 12 \\ P_1 & =⟨12 t - 4,\,54 t^{2} - 18 t,\,- 24 t^{3} + 18 t - 12⟩ \\ P_2 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 9 t^{2} & - 4 t & -3 \\ 9 t^{2} & - 4 t & -3\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{2,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}- 4 t & -3 \\ - 4 t & -3\end{vmatrix}=0 \\ P_{2,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}9 t^{2} & -3 \\ 9 t^{2} & -3\end{vmatrix}=0 \\ P_{2,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}9 t^{2} & - 4 t \\ 9 t^{2} & - 4 t\end{vmatrix}=0 \\ P_2 & =⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(f^{\prime}\times f)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =⟨12 t - 4,\,54 t^{2} - 18 t,\,- 24 t^{3} + 18 t - 12⟩\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u\\2 u^{2} + v^{2}\\- v\end{pmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u)&=1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(2 u^{2} + v^{2})&=4 u\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(2 u^{2} + v^{2})&=2 v\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- v)&=-1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}1\\4 u\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\2 v\\-1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1 & 4 u & 0\\0 & 2 v & -1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(4 u)(-1)\\&\quad -(0)(2 v)\\&=- 4 u.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(1)(-1)\\&\quad +(0)(0)\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(1)(2 v)\\&\quad -(4 u)(0)\\&=2 v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}- 4 u\\1\\2 v\end{pmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u^{2}\\\sin{(v )}\\- 2 u \cos{(v )}\end{pmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u^{2})&=2 u\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\sin{(v )})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- 2 u \cos{(v )})&=- 2 \cos{(v )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u^{2})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(\sin{(v )})&=\cos{(v )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- 2 u \cos{(v )})&=2 u \sin{(v )}\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}2 u\\0\\- 2 \cos{(v )}\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\cos{(v )}\\2 u \sin{(v )}\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2 u & 0 & - 2 \cos{(v )}\\0 & \cos{(v )} & 2 u \sin{(v )}\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(0)(2 u \sin{(v )})\\&\quad -(- 2 \cos{(v )})(\cos{(v )})\\&=2 \cos^{2}{(v )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(2 u)(2 u \sin{(v )})\\&\quad +(- 2 \cos{(v )})(0)\\&=- 4 u^{2} \sin{(v )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(2 u)(\cos{(v )})\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=2 u \cos{(v )}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}2 \cos^{2}{(v )}\\- 4 u^{2} \sin{(v )}\\2 u \cos{(v )}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the parametric surface

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u + 1,v,- 2 u - v\rangle.
$$

For $-2\le u\le 0$ and $1\le v\le 4$.

The tangent vectors are $\mathbf r_u=\langle 1,0,-2\rangle$ and $\mathbf r_v=\langle 0,1,-1\rangle$. Use

$$
A(S)=\iint_D\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\mathrm dA.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization over $D$, use $$
A(S)=\iint_D\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\mathrm dA
$$

Differentiate and form the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,0,-2\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 0,1,-1\rangle,\\\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&0&-2\\0&1&-1\end{vmatrix}\\&=\langle 2,1,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|=\sqrt{(2)^2+(1)^2+(1)^2}=\sqrt{6}.
$$

The parameter rectangle has side lengths $0-(-2)=2$ and $4-(1)=3$, so its area is $6$.

The area scale factor is constant, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(S)&=\iint_D \sqrt{6}\,\mathrm dA\\&=\sqrt{6}\cdot\operatorname{Area}(D)\\&=\sqrt{6}\cdot(6)=6 \sqrt{6}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $u(r,\theta)=- 3 r^{3}$, find $\frac{∂u}{∂x}$, where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂x}=\frac{∂u}{∂r}\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}\sin \theta.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂r}=- 9 r^{2},\,\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =(- 9 r^{2})\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}(0)\sin \theta \\ & =- 9 r^{2} \cos {\theta}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\iint_D\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\,\mathrm dA
$$

$$
D=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 1,\ 0\le v\le 2\}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle v,\,u,\,u - 4 v\rangle
$$

for $(u,v)\in D$.

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 0,\,1,\,1\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,0,\,-4\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The surface-area integrand is the magnitude of the fundamental vector product:

$$
A(S)=\iint_D \left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Differentiate each coordinate with respect to each parameter:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 0,\,1,\,1\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,0,\,-4\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Expand the determinant to find the cross product:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -4\end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\langle -4,\,1,\,-1\rangle
$$

Square the components, add, and take the nonnegative square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|^2&=\left(-4\right)^2+\left(1\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(-1\right)^2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|&=\sqrt{18} \\ &=3 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the required integral is

$$
A(S)=\iint_D 3 \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm dA.
$$

The missing expression is $3 \sqrt{2}$. The integral does not need to be evaluated.

\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 0,\,e^{v} \cos{\left(u \right)},\,- e^{v} \sin{\left(u \right)}\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v&=\langle 5,\,e^{v} \sin{\left(u \right)},\,e^{v} \cos{\left(u \right)}\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Expand the determinant to find the cross product:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 0 & e^{v} \cos{\left(u \right)} & - e^{v} \sin{\left(u \right)} \\ 5 & e^{v} \sin{\left(u \right)} & e^{v} \cos{\left(u \right)}\end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}c_1&=e^{2 v} \sin^{2}{\left(u \right)} + e^{2 v} \cos^{2}{\left(u \right)}=e^{2 v} \\ c_2&=- 5 e^{v} \sin{\left(u \right)} \\ c_3&=- 5 e^{v} \cos{\left(u \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\langle e^{2 v},\,- 5 e^{v} \sin{\left(u \right)},\,- 5 e^{v} \cos{\left(u \right)}\rangle
$$

Use $\sin^{2}{\left(u \right)}+\cos^{2}{\left(u \right)}=1$ to combine the squared trigonometric terms.

Square the components, add, and take the nonnegative square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|^2&=\left(e^{2 v}\right)^2+\left(- 5 e^{v} \sin{\left(u \right)}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(- 5 e^{v} \cos{\left(u \right)}\right)^2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|&=\sqrt{e^{4 v} + 25 e^{2 v}} \\ &=\sqrt{\left(e^{2 v} + 25\right) e^{2 v}} \\ &=\sqrt{e^{2 v} + 25} e^{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Exponential factors are positive, so their squared factors have positive square roots.

Thus the required integral is

$$
A(S)=\iint_D \sqrt{e^{2 v} + 25} e^{v}\,\mathrm dA.
$$

The missing expression is $\sqrt{e^{2 v} + 25} e^{v}$. The integral does not need to be evaluated.

question.:question/problem:
$$
\iint_D\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\,\mathrm dA
$$

$$
D=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 2,\ 0\le v\le 4\}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle 2 u^{2},\,v^{2},\,u v\rangle
$$

for $(u,v)\in D$.

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The surface-area integrand is the magnitude of the fundamental vector product:

$$
A(S)=\iint_D \left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Differentiate each coordinate with respect to each parameter:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 4 u,\,0,\,v\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v&=\langle 0,\,2 v,\,u\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Expand the determinant to find the cross product:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 4 u & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2 v & u\end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\langle - 2 v^{2},\,- 4 u^{2},\,8 u v\rangle
$$

Square the components, add, and take the nonnegative square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|^2&=\left(- 2 v^{2}\right)^2+\left(- 4 u^{2}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(8 u v\right)^2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|&=\sqrt{16 u^{4} + 64 u^{2} v^{2} + 4 v^{4}} \\ &=\sqrt{4 \left(4 u^{4} + 16 u^{2} v^{2} + v^{4}\right)} \\ &=2 \sqrt{4 u^{4} + 16 u^{2} v^{2} + v^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the required integral is

$$
A(S)=\iint_D 2 \sqrt{4 u^{4} + 16 u^{2} v^{2} + v^{4}}\,\mathrm dA.
$$

The missing expression is $2 \sqrt{4 u^{4} + 16 u^{2} v^{2} + v^{4}}$. The integral does not need to be evaluated.

$$

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 0 & 2 v \cos{\left(u \right)} & - v \sin{\left(u \right)} \\ 2 v & 2 \sin{\left(u \right)} & \cos{\left(u \right)}\end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}c_1&=2 v \sin^{2}{\left(u \right)} + 2 v \cos^{2}{\left(u \right)}=2 v \\ c_2&=- 2 v^{2} \sin{\left(u \right)} \\ c_3&=- 4 v^{2} \cos{\left(u \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\langle 2 v,\,- 2 v^{2} \sin{\left(u \right)},\,- 4 v^{2} \cos{\left(u \right)}\rangle
$$

$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=8xy+4{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\sin\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\cos\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=8y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=8x+8y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =8r\sin\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =8r\cos\theta +8r\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta} & =-8r\sin\theta \,r\sin\theta +(8r\cos\theta +8r\sin\theta )r\cos\theta  \\ & =8{r}^{2}(\cos^{2}\theta -\sin^{2}\theta )+4{r}^{2}\sin(2\theta) \\ & =8{r}^{2}\cos(2\theta)+4{r}^{2}\sin(2\theta)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x, y) = 3\ln(x+y)$, find $\frac{∂g}{∂r}$, where $(x, y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r, \theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cos\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{3}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{3}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{3}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{3}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{3}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta })\cos\theta +(\frac{3}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta })\sin\theta  \\ & =\frac{3(\cos\theta +\sin\theta )}{r(\cos\theta +\sin\theta )} \\ & =\frac{3}{r}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y - 2 y^{2},$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =(\frac{∂w}{∂x})(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})+(\frac{∂w}{∂y})(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=- 6 x + 4 y,\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=4 x - 4 y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} - 6 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =- 4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =(4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} - 6 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)})(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})+(- 4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)})(\sin{\left(\theta \right)}) \\  & =(4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} - 6 r \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)})+(- 4 r \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}) \\  & =- 4 r \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} + 8 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} - 6 r \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =- 2 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 8 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} - 2 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}.\end{aligned}

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=- 4 x^{4}$ and $v(x)=\tan{\left(x \right)}.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}(u(x)v(x))' &=u'(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot v'(x) \\ &=(- 4 x^{4})'\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)}) \\ &\quad +(- 4 x^{4})\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)})' \\ &=(- 16 x^{3})(\tan{\left(x \right)}) \\ &\quad +(- 4 x^{4})(\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}) \\ &=- 16 x^{3} \tan{\left(x \right)} \\ &\quad +(- 4 x^{4} \sec^{2}{\left(x \right)})\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Find $\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}$, where

$$
u(t)=\ln{\left(t \right)},\qquad \mathbf f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}- t^{3} \\ t^{2} \\ 2 t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Assume $t>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar function multiple rule:

$$
\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}(t)\mathbf f(t)+u(t)\mathbf f^{\prime}(t).
$$

Differentiate the scalar and each vector component.

$$
u^{\prime}(t)=\frac{1}{t}.
$$



$$
\mathbf f^{\prime}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}- 3 t^{2} \\ 2 t \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Substitute both contributions and add corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}&=\big(\frac{1}{t}\big)\begin{bmatrix}- t^{3} \\ t^{2} \\ 2 t\end{bmatrix}\\&\quad+\big(\ln{\left(t \right)}\big)\begin{bmatrix}- 3 t^{2} \\ 2 t \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $\mathbf h(t)=u(t)\mathbf f(t)$. For each component, the two terms are:

$$
\begin{aligned}h_{1}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(- t^{2}\big)\\&\quad+\big(- 3 t^{2} \ln{\left(t \right)}\big)\\&=- 3 t^{2} \ln{\left(t \right)} - t^{2}\\h_{2}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(t\big)\\&\quad+\big(2 t \ln{\left(t \right)}\big)\\&=2 t \ln{\left(t \right)} + t\\h_{3}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(2\big)\\&\quad+\big(2 \ln{\left(t \right)}\big)\\&=2 \ln{\left(t \right)} + 2.\end{aligned}
$$

 Therefore,

$$
\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}- 3 t^{2} \ln{\left(t \right)} - t^{2} \\ 2 t \ln{\left(t \right)} + t \\ 2 \ln{\left(t \right)} + 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}(t)\mathbf f(t)+u(t)\mathbf f^{\prime}(t).
$$

Differentiate the scalar and each vector component.

$$
u^{\prime}(t)=-2.
$$



$$
\mathbf f^{\prime}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 6 t^{2} \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.

Substitute both contributions and add corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}&=\big(-2\big)\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 t^{3} \\ - t\end{bmatrix}\\&\quad+\big(- 2 t - 2\big)\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 6 t^{2} \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $\mathbf h(t)=u(t)\mathbf f(t)$. For each component, the two terms are:

$$
\begin{aligned}h_{1}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(2\big)\\&\quad+\big(0\big)\\&=2\\h_{2}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(- 4 t^{3}\big)\\&\quad+\big(6 t^{2} \left(- 2 t - 2\right)\big)\\&=- 16 t^{3} - 12 t^{2}\\h_{3}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(2 t\big)\\&\quad+\big(2 t + 2\big)\\&=4 t + 2.\end{aligned}

 Therefore,

$$

$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=(- 3 e^{x})\cdot (1)+(x - 1)\cdot (- 3 e^{x}) \\ &=- 3 x e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=0} &=\begin{aligned}&(- 3 e^{(0)})\cdot (1) \\ &{}+((0) - 1)\cdot (- 3 e^{(0)})\end{aligned} \\ &=(-3)\cdot (1)+(-1)\cdot (-3) \\ &=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $0.$

question.:question/problem: Which inequality corresponds to the interval $t\in [-6,-5]$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $(,)$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

Our interval contains only brackets. So, the endpoints *are* included. 

$$
t\in [-6,-5]
$$

Therefore, our interval can be expressed as the following inequality:

$$
-5
\,\,\ge \,\,t\,\,\ge \,\,
-6
$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying Independence of Parametrization and Orientation

question.:question/problem:
The paths $C$ and $D$ trace exactly the same geometric arc once, in opposite directions. The path $D=-C$ is the reversed path in the diagram.

![The same curve traversed in opposite directions.](images/e4/e4f68e10429fa4bda69366751c303216d27df995edf2502b61ab9bfe84c3ff45.png)

The parametrization of $D$ runs 3 times as fast, with its parameter interval shortened accordingly. Suppose $f$ is continuous along the arc and

$$
\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=2.
$$

What is the value of $\int_{D} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Scalar line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of parametrization and orientation. Both paths cover the same arc once, so

$$
\int_{D} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=2.
$$

The speed change is offset by the shortened parameter interval. Reversing direction does not negate the integral, and a single traversal does not cancel it. Neither multiplying nor dividing by the parameter speed is appropriate.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C_2$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_2(t)=\langle 2\cos(t),2\sin(t)\rangle
$$

for $0\le t\le \pi$. The curve $C_1$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_1(u)=\langle 2\cos(\pi-3u),2\sin(\pi-3u)\rangle
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac{1}{3}\pi$. Suppose $f$ is continuous along both curves and

$$
\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-4.
$$

A minus sign on a curve means its orientation is reversed. **Which statements must be true** for every such $f$? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write points on the known curve in terms of a geometric parameter $z$:

$$
\mathbf R(z)=\langle 2\cos(z),2\sin(z)\rangle.
$$

For $C_2$, $z=t$ increases from $0$ to $\pi$. For $C_1$, $z=\pi-3u$ decreases from $\pi$ to $0$. Eliminating the parameter on $C_2$ gives $x^2+y^2=4,\quad y\ge0$. The other curve has the same locus, branch and full parameter range; both traverse the arc once. The parameter map is $t=(\pi-3u)/1$. Its sign controls direction, not the scalar integral. 

Reversing $C_2$ always preserves its value:

$$
\int_{-C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-4.
$$

Independence of parametrization and orientation also gives $\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-4$. Changing the parameter speed does not supply a multiplicative factor. 

Statement 1, $\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-4$, is **true**. Statement 2, $\int_{-C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-4$, is **true**. Statement 3, $\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=4$, is **not guaranteed**.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C_1$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_1(t)=\langle 3(t)^4-3(t)^2,(t)\rangle
$$

for $0\le t\le 2$. The curve $C_2$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_2(u)=\langle 3(2u)^4-3(2u)^2,(2u)\rangle
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac{1}{2}$. Suppose $f$ is continuous along both curves and

$$
\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=8.
$$

A minus sign on a curve means its orientation is reversed. **Which statements must be true** for every such $f$? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write points on the known curve in terms of a geometric parameter $z$:

$$
\mathbf R(z)=\langle 3(z)^4-3(z)^2,(z)\rangle.
$$

For $C_1$, $z=t$ increases from $0$ to $2$. For $C_2$, $z=2u$ increases from $0$ to $1$. Eliminating the parameter on $C_1$ gives $x=3y^4-3y^2$. The other curve covers only the part with $0\le z\le 1$, rather than $0\le z\le 2$. A shared Cartesian equation alone is insufficient. A continuous function supported near an interior point of the omitted arc can be scaled to give any prescribed nonzero integral on the full curve, while its integral on the subarc stays zero. Thus no nonzero fixed multiple of the full integral is guaranteed on the subarc. 

Reversing $C_1$ always preserves its value:

$$
\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=8.
$$

Changing the parameter speed does not supply a multiplicative factor. 

Statement 1, $\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=4$, is **not guaranteed**. Statement 2, $\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=8$, is **true**. Statement 3, $\int_{-C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=8$, is **not guaranteed**.

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y,z)=2 x - 3 y + z$ and $r(t)=(t)\,i+(t^{2})\,j+(t^{2})\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2 x - 3 y + z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2 x - 3 y + z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2 x - 3 y + z)\,k \\  & =(2)\,i+(-3)\,j+(1)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y=t^{2},$ and $z=t^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2)\,i+(-3)\,j+(1)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})\,k \\  & =(1)\,i+(2 t)\,j+(2 t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2)\,i+(-3)\,j+(1)\,k)\cdot ((1)\,i+(2 t)\,j+(2 t)\,k) \\  & =(2)\cdot (1)+(-3)\cdot (2 t)+(1)\cdot (2 t) \\  & =(2)+(- 6 t)+(2 t) \\  & =2 \left(1 - 2 t\right).\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Volume of a Parallelepiped Spanned by Three Vectors

question.:question/worked-solution:
The volume is the absolute value of the scalar triple product of the actual edge vectors. Use those edges as the determinant rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D&=\begin{vmatrix}-2&1&-4\\-3&2&0\\-1&3&-1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2&0\\3&-1\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad -1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-3&0\\-1&-1\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad +(-4)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-3&2\\-1&3\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-2)(2\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 3)\\
&\quad -1((-3)\cdot (-1)-0\cdot (-1))\\
&\quad +(-4)((-3)\cdot 3-2\cdot (-1))\\
&=4+(-3)+28=29.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, take the absolute value:

$$
V=|29|=29.
$$

$V=${{volume}}

The volume is the magnitude of the scalar triple product of the actual edges. Factor each edge scale out separately. An even number of pairwise swaps preserves the triple product.

$$

\end{aligned}
$$

Take the absolute value:

$$
V=|42|=42.
$$

First form the actual edge vectors component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}

&=\langle 3-1,0-(-2),(-1)-0\rangle\\
&=\langle 2,2,-1\rangle.\\
\mathbf{v}&=\mathbf{b}\\
&=\langle 1,(-2),0\rangle\\
&=\langle 1,-2,0\rangle.\\
\mathbf{w}&=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c}\\
&=\langle 3+(-2),0+1,(-1)+2\rangle\\
&=\langle 1,1,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The volume is the absolute value of the scalar triple product of the actual edge vectors. Use those edges as the determinant rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D&=\begin{vmatrix}2&2&-1\\1&-2&0\\1&1&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-2&0\\1&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad -2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad +(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1&-2\\1&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=2((-2)\cdot 1-0\cdot 1)\\
&\quad -2(1\cdot 1-0\cdot 1)\\
&\quad +(-1)(1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 1)\\
&=(-4)+(-2)+(-3)=-9.
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Volume of a Parallelepiped Spanned by Three Vectors

question.:question/problem:
Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}&=\langle -2,-1,1\rangle,\\
\mathbf{b}&=\langle -2,-3,2\rangle,\\
\mathbf{c}&=\langle -1,1,-2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped whose three edge vectors are

$$
\mathbf{b},\quad \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c},\quad \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}.
$$

$V=${{volume}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First form the actual edge vectors component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{u}&=\mathbf{b}\\
&=\langle (-2),(-3),2\rangle\\
&=\langle -2,-3,2\rangle.\\
\mathbf{v}&=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c}\\
&=\langle (-2)+(-1),(-1)+1,1+(-2)\rangle\\
&=\langle -3,0,-1\rangle.\\
\mathbf{w}&=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\\
&=\langle (-2)+(-2),(-1)+(-3),1+2\rangle\\
&=\langle -4,-4,3\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The volume is the absolute value of the scalar triple product of the actual edge vectors. Use those edges as the determinant rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D&=\begin{vmatrix}-2&-3&2\\-3&0&-1\\-4&-4&3\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0&-1\\-4&3\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad -(-3)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-3&-1\\-4&3\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad +2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-3&0\\-4&-4\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-2)(0\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-4))\\
&\quad -(-3)((-3)\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-4))\\
&\quad +2((-3)\cdot (-4)-0\cdot (-4))\\
&=8+(-39)+24=-7.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, take the absolute value:

$$
V=|-7|=7.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{u}&=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}\\
&=\langle (-1)-1,(-1)-2,3-(-1)\rangle\\

&=\langle (-2)+(-1),(-1)+(-1),(-3)+3\rangle\\

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} - 3 y^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨t - 2,2 t + 1⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2 x^{2} - 3 y^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(2 x^{2} - 3 y^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨4 x,- 6 y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t - 2$, $y=2 t + 1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨4 \left(t - 2\right),- 6 \left(2 t + 1\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨4 t - 8,- 12 t - 6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t - 2),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨4 t - 8,- 12 t - 6⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\  & =\left(4 t - 8\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(- 12 t - 6\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\  & =- 20 t - 20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =- 20 (1) - 20 \\  & =-40.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=- 3 x y z$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨- t,\sqrt{t},- t + 3⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(- 3 x y z),\frac{∂}{∂y}(- 3 x y z),\frac{∂}{∂z}(- 3 x y z)⟩ \\  & =⟨- 3 y z,- 3 x z,- 3 x y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=- t$, $y=\sqrt{t}$, $z=- t + 3$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨- 3 \sqrt{t} \left(- t + 3\right),- 3 \left(- t\right) \left(- t + 3\right),- 3 \sqrt{t} \left(- t\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨3 t^{\frac{3}{2}} - 9 \sqrt{t},- 3 t^{2} + 9 t,3 t^{\frac{3}{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t + 3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t}},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨3 t^{\frac{3}{2}} - 9 \sqrt{t},- 3 t^{2} + 9 t,3 t^{\frac{3}{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t}},-1⟩ \\  & =\left(3 t^{\frac{3}{2}} - 9 \sqrt{t}\right)\cdot \left(-1\right)+\left(- 3 t^{2} + 9 t\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t}}\right)+\left(3 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\  & =3 \sqrt{t} \left(- t + 3\right)+\frac{3 \sqrt{t} \left(- t + 3\right)}{2}- 3 t^{\frac{3}{2}} \\  & =\frac{3 \sqrt{t} \left(- 5 t + 9\right)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{3 \sqrt{(1)} \left(- 5 (1) + 9\right)}{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Volume of a Parallelepiped Spanned by Three Position Vectors Given Their Coordinates

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}$, and $\overrightarrow{AD}$, given

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(-2,2,0),&\quad B(1,2,3),\\
C(-5,-1,-1),&\quad D(-3,3,-3).
\end{aligned}
$$

Select the volume in cubic units.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Subtract the common vertex $A$ from each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{AB}&=\langle1-(-2),2-2,3-0\rangle=\langle3,0,3\rangle\\
\overrightarrow{AC}&=\langle-5-(-2),-1-2,-1-0\rangle=\langle-3,-3,-1\rangle\\
\overrightarrow{AD}&=\langle-3-(-2),3-2,-3-0\rangle=\langle-1,1,-3\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the scalar triple product:

$T=\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{AD})$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -3\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Expand along row $1$, whose cofactor signs are $+,-,+$. Zero entries make no contribution. Evaluate the needed minors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_1&=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-3)\cdot(-3)-(-1)\cdot1=10\\
M_3&=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-3)\cdot1-(-3)\cdot(-1)=-6
\end{aligned}
$$

Combine the signed contributions before taking the absolute value:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=3M_1+3M_3\\
&=3\cdot10+3\cdot(-6)\\
&=30+(-18)=12
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
V&=|12|=12\text{ cubic units}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
![Curve and its measurements](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-28-topic-audit-3/group-2/generator-runtime/17592186162081/easy/output/e366ceb3fe9d4cea3cf4ac5a81dfbde78648896aebd7f3801317611f4b447561.png)

Calculate

$$
\int_C\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is the semicircular arc with radius $7$ shown, traversed once counterclockwise. The dashed guide is not part of the path.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length equals the length $L$ of the path:

$$
\int_C\,\mathrm{d}s=L.
$$

The supplied radius determines the diameter:

$$
d=2r=2(7)=14.
$$

The path is half of a circle. Using circumference from diameter,

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\frac{\pi d}{2}\\&=\frac{\pi(14)}{2}=7 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C\,\mathrm{d}s=7 \pi.
$$

Reversing the direction leaves traveled length unchanged.

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,-2)$ for the curve $5 x^{2} - 2 y^{3}=36$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Apply the power rule and the chain rule, treating $y$ as a function of $x$.

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, then collect the derivative terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}\left(5 x^{2} - 2 y^{3}\right)&=\frac{d}{dx}\left(36\right)\\
- 6 \frac{dy}{dx} y^{2} + 10 x&=0\\
\left(- 6 y^{2}\right)\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\left(10 x\right)\\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{10 x}{- 6 y^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

At $(2,-2)$, the coefficient of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is $-24\ne 0$. Substitute the point to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
m&=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(2,-2)}\\
&=-\frac{20}{-24}\\
&=\frac{5}{6}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Treat $y$ as a function of $x$. Differentiate implicitly and collect the derivative terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 x+\left(6 y\right)\frac{dy}{dx}&=0 \\
\left(6 y\right)\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\left(2 x\right) \\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{2 x}{6 y}
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope at the given point:

$$
m_{\mathrm{t}}=-\frac{2}{18}=- \frac{1}{9}
$$

The tangent line uses $m=- \frac{1}{9}$.

Use the given point and this slope:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-\left(3\right)&=- \frac{1}{9}\left(x-\left(1\right)\right) \\
y&=- \frac{1}{9}\left(x-\left(1\right)\right)+\left(3\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=- \frac{1}{9}\left(x-\left(1\right)\right)+\left(3\right) \\

\end{aligned}

x&=-4
\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
The function

$$
f(t,z)=\langle \text{_____},\,4\tan t,\,z\rangle
$$

with $-\pi/2<t<\pi/2$ and $z\in\mathbb R$ parametrizes the sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder

$$
\frac{x^2}{1}-\frac{y^2}{16}=1,\qquad x\ge 1.
$$

Use $\sec^2 t-\tan^2 t=1$. What is the first component of $f$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The equation is already normalized. The base curve uses $x$ and $y$; $z$ is the free coordinate. Substituting the supplied component gives

$$
\frac{x^2}{1}=1+\frac{(4\tan t)^2}{16}=1+\tan^2 t=\sec^2 t.
$$

Since $x\ge 1$ and $\sec t\ge1$ on the given interval, take the positive root. The scale is $1=\sqrt{1}$. Thus

$$
x=\sec t,\qquad f(t,z)=\langle \sec t,\,4\tan t,\,z\rangle.
$$

Check in the normalized equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(\sec t)^2}{1}-\frac{(4\tan t)^2}{16}&=\sec^2 t-\tan^2 t\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

The secant coordinate satisfies the positive-sheet condition. The tangent coordinate ranges over all real values, and arbitrary real $z$ extends the base curve along the cylinder axis. Therefore the first component is $\sec t$.

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ for $3 x^{3} y + y^{2}=3 x^{2} + 1$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as a function of $x$ and write $y'=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$. Use the **product rule** for each mixed product, including the chain-rule factor $y^{\prime}$ when differentiating a function of $y$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(3 x^{3} y\right)&=3 x^{3} y' + 9 x^{2} y
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate the equation, collect all terms containing $y^{\prime}$, and factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
9 x^{2} y + y' \left(3 x^{3} + 2 y\right)&=6 x\\
\left(3 x^{3} + 2 y\right)y^{\prime}&=- 9 x^{2} y + 6 x
\end{aligned}
$$

Divide by the coefficient of $y^{\prime}$:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{- 9 x^{2} y + 6 x}{3 x^{3} + 2 y}
$$

This formula applies where $3 x^{3} + 2 y\ne0$.

question.:question/problem: Given that $-12a + 9b$ and $\lambda (-8a + 6b)$ are equal (non-zero) vectors, find the scale factor $\lambda .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the vectors are equal, we can write

$$
-12a + 9b=\lambda (-8a + 6b).
$$

Next, we factor the left-hand side, which gives

$$
\frac{3}{2}(-8a + 6b)=\lambda (-8a + 6b).
$$

Notice that we have $(-8a + 6b)$ on both sides. So, let's define a new vector $u$ as

$$
u=-8a + 6b.
$$

Then, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{3}{2}\,u=\lambda u.
$$

Since $u$ is non-zero,

$$
\lambda=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

The line segment $\overline{XY}$ is a diameter of a circle. Given that $X$ and $Y$ have coordinates $(1,2)$ and $(1,-6)$, respectively, what is the equation of the circle?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The general equation of a circle with radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ is

$$
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2.
$$

Using the distance formula to compute the distance between the points $X(1,2)$ and $Y(1,-6),$ we find that the length of the diameter is

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{(1-1)^2+(2-(-6))^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^2+(8)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{0+64} \\  & =\sqrt{64} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So the radius of the circle is

$$
r=\frac{XY}{2}=\frac{8}{2}=4.
$$

Since the center of a circle is the midpoint of the diameter, to find the center we use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{y_1+y_2}{2})=(\frac{1+1}{2},\frac{2+(-6)}{2})=(1,-2)
$$

So our circle has radius $r=4$ and center $(a,b)=(1,-2),$ and therefore it is represented by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 & =r^2 \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y-(-2))^{2} & =(4)^2 \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y+2)^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=2$ given that $∇f(x,y)=\left(\frac{2 x}{x^{2} + 4 y}\right)\,i+\left(\frac{4}{x^{2} + 4 y}\right)\,j$ and $r(t)=\left(4 t\right)\,i+\left(2 t^{2}\right)\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\left(\frac{2 x}{x^{2} + 4 y}\right)\,i+\left(\frac{4}{x^{2} + 4 y}\right)\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=4 t$ and $y=2 t^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\left(\frac{2 x}{x^{2} + 4 y}\right)\,i+\left(\frac{4}{x^{2} + 4 y}\right)\,j\Big|_{x=4 t,\,y=2 t^{2}} \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{3 t}\right)\,i+\left(\frac{1}{6 t^{2}}\right)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(4 t\right)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(2 t^{2}\right)\,j \\  & =\left(4\right)\,i+\left(4 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{1}{3 t}\right)\,i+\left(\frac{1}{6 t^{2}}\right)\,j\right)\cdot \left(\left(4\right)\,i+\left(4 t\right)\,j\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{3 t}\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(\frac{1}{6 t^{2}}\right)\cdot \left(4 t\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{4}{3 t}\right)+\left(\frac{2}{3 t}\right) \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]\Big|_{t=2} & =\frac{2}{t}\Big|_{t=2} \\  & =\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]\Big|_{t=\frac{5 \pi}{8}} & =- \sin{\left(4 t \right)} + 8 \cos^{2}{\left(2 t \right)} - 4\Big|_{t=\frac{5 \pi}{8}} \\  & =\left(4\right)+\left(-5\right) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\left(3 x + 3 y\right)\,i+\left(3 x + 3 y\right)\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\sin{\left(t \right)}$ and $y=\cos{\left(t \right)}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\left(3 x + 3 y\right)\,i+\left(3 x + 3 y\right)\,j\Big|_{x=\sin{\left(t \right)},\,y=\cos{\left(t \right)}} \\  & =\left(3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\,i+\left(3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\,j \\  & =\left(\cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =\left(\left(3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\,i+\left(3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\,j\right)\cdot \left(\left(\cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\,j\right) \\  & =\left(3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\  & =\left(3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(- 3 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \sin{\left(t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right) \\  & =3 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi}{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]\Big|_{t=\frac{\pi}{4}} & =3 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\Big|_{t=\frac{\pi}{4}} \\  & =\left(3\right)+\left(-3\right) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$

$$

First, we substitute $x=\sin{\left(3 t \right)}$ and $y=\cos{\left(3 t \right)}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\left(3 x + 2 y\right)\,i+\left(2 x + 2 y\right)\,j\Big|_{x=\sin{\left(3 t \right)},\,y=\cos{\left(3 t \right)}} \\  & =\left(3 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(2 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(3 t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\sin{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,j \\  & =\left(3 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(- 3 \sin{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =\left(\left(3 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(2 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(3 t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\,j\right)\cdot \left(\left(3 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(- 3 \sin{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\,j\right) \\  & =\left(3 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right)\cdot \left(3 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right)+\left(2 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(3 t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(- 3 \sin{\left(3 t \right)}\right) \\  & =\left(9 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} \cos{\left(3 t \right)} + 6 \cos^{2}{\left(3 t \right)}\right)+\left(- 6 \sqrt{2} \sin{\left(3 t \right)} \sin{\left(3 t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\right) \\  & =\frac{3 \left(\sin{\left(6 t \right)} + 4 \cos{\left(6 t \right)}\right)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the period of the function

$$
f(x)=-\cos\left(\frac{4}{3}x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+1.
$$

Angles are measured in radians.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Read the coefficient of $x$ inside the cosine:

$$
B=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

The period is a positive length. One full turn is $2\pi$ in radians.

$$

The outside multiplier and the constant shifts do not change the period.

question.:question/problem:
Which ordinary definite integral represents $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(- y^{2})\,i+(2 x^{2})\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(t^{2})\,i+(t)\,j$ for $t\in [0,2]$?

Use the supplied parameterization and limits. Select the integral whose integrand is $F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)$; do not evaluate it.

*Hint: $r^{\prime}(t)=(2 t)\,i+(1)\,j$. Substitute both coordinates into the field, then take the dot product.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the vector line-integral formula:

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Substitute the coordinates $x=t^{2}$ and $y=t$ into both field components:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))&=(- (t)^{2})\,i\\&\quad+(2 (t^{2})^{2})\,j\\&=(- t^{2})\,i\\&\quad+(2 t^{4})\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each path component:

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{2})=2 t,\\y^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply matching components and add:

$$
\begin{aligned}&F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\\&=(- t^{2})(2 t)\\&\quad+(2 t^{4})(1).\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the products:

$$
F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)=2 t^{4} - 2 t^{3}.
$$

Keep the supplied parameter limits. The required integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{0}^{2}\bigl[(- t^{2})(2 t)\\&\quad+(2 t^{4})(1)\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

reverse second field component; swap derivatives

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Midline of a Transformed Sinusoidal Function

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the midline for a transformed sine function with a minimum value of $-1$ and a maximum value of $5$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The midline is the horizontal line halfway between the minimum and maximum values. Average their heights:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \frac{y_{\text{min}}+y_{\text{max}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{-1+5}{2} \\
&= 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=2$. The half-range $3$ is the amplitude, rather than the vertical shift.

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating Surface Integrals

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
\iint_S 4\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x + 2 y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x + 2 y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x + 2 y)=2.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$

$$

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sin{\left(x + y \right)})=\cos{\left(x + y \right)},
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sin{\left(x + y \right)})=\cos{\left(x + y \right)}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{2 z}{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}}{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}\sqrt{1+\left(\cos{\left(x + y \right)}\right)^{2}+\left(\cos{\left(x + y \right)}\right)^{2}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}}{\cancel{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}}\cancel{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}\,\text{d}A\\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\int_{- x}^{x}\left(2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}\right)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}[- 2 \cos{\left(x + y \right)}]_{y=- x}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x\\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\left(4 \sin^{2}{\left(x \right)}\right)\,\text{d}x\\ & =[(2 x)+(- \sin{\left(2 x \right)})]_{x=0}^{x=\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\\ & =\left((3 \pi)+(0)-\left((0)+(0)\right)\right)\\ & =3 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](17592186105888/easy/17592186105888/plots/275ce1a3e1be0f890bbb6980c0e3f4a3b0cf0ed668a0dc1874278166cc977777.png)

Evaluate the surface integral

$$\iint_S 5\,\mathrm{d}S,$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x + y$ and whose domain is the disk of radius $2$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x + y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x + y)=1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{5}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(5)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(5)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{5}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 2,\ 0\le\theta\le 2 \pi\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{5}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(5)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{5 r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\int_{0}^{2}{5 r}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[\frac{5 r^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[((10))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{10}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(10 \sqrt{3})\left[\theta\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ & =(10 \sqrt{3})\left[((2 \pi))-((0))\right] \\ & =(10 \sqrt{3})\cdot((2 \pi)-(0)) \\ & =20 \sqrt{3} \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $20 \sqrt{3} \pi$.

The sides $CA=8$ and $CB=18$ meet at $C$, so $43^{\circ}$ is their included angle.

&=72\sin 43^{\circ}\\
&\approx 49.10388192\\
&\approx 49.10.
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Express Surface Integrals as Repeated Integrals

question.:question/problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=- x z,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2 x + 2 y$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 0.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}\,\boxed{}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2 x + 2 y)=2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(2 x + 2 y)=2.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+(2)^2+(2)^2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(- x (2 x + 2 y))\cdot (3)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(- 2 x^{2} - 2 x y)\cdot (3)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}\,- 6 x^{2} - 6 x y\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

The diagram shows $A$ and $B$ on a circle centered at the origin $O$. Point $A$ has polar coordinates $(9,150^\circ)$ and the marked angle is $\angle AOB=90^\circ$.

Moving from $A$ to $B$ along the marked arc is counterclockwise, so add the marked angle. Use $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ to find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$.

Which ordered pair gives the Cartesian coordinates of $B$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Both points lie on the same circle, so $B$ has radius $9$. Along the marked arc, moving from $A$ to $B$ is counterclockwise; add the marked angle.

$$
\theta_B=150^\circ+90^\circ=240^\circ.
$$

Thus $B$ has polar coordinates $(9,240^\circ)$. Using $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &=9\cos\left(240^\circ\right)=9\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)=- \frac{9}{2},\\y &=9\sin\left(240^\circ\right)=9\left(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(- \frac{9}{2},- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{2})$.

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ given that $F(x,y,z)=\left(- z\right)\,i+\left(2 x\right)\,j+\left(2 y\right)\,k$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(2 t + 1\right)\,j+\left(2 t - 1\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1]$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=t,\qquad y=2 t + 1,\qquad z=2 t - 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- z\,i+2 x\,j+2 y\,k \\ & =\left(- \left(2 t - 1\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 \left(t\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 \left(2 t + 1\right)\right)\,k \\ & =\left(1 - 2 t\right)\,i+2 t\,j+\left(4 t + 2\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t + 1\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t - 1\right)\,k \\ & =\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(1 - 2 t\right)\left(1\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 t\right)\left(2\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(4 t + 2\right)\left(2\right) \\ & =\left(1\right)+\left(- 2 t\right)+\left(4 t\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(4\right)+\left(8 t\right) \\ & =10 t + 5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(10 t + 5\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[5 t^{2} + 5 t\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(5 \left(1\right)^{2} + 5 \left(1\right)\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(5 \left(0\right)^{2} + 5 \left(0\right)\right)\right) \\ & =\left(10\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =10\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- 2 y\,i+- x\,j+- z\,k \\ & =\left(- 2 \left(1 - t\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- \left(2 t - 1\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(- \left(- 2 t\right)\right)\,k \\ & =\left(2 t - 2\right)\,i+\left(1 - 2 t\right)\,j+2 t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t - 1\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(1 - t\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- 2 t\right)\,k \\ & =2\,i+-\,j+-2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(2 t - 5\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[t^{2} - 5 t\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(\left(1\right)^{2} - 5 \left(1\right)\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(\left(0\right)^{2} - 5 \left(0\right)\right)\right) \\ & =\left(-4\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\sec{\left(t \right)}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\,k \\ & =2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,i \\ &\quad {}+\tan{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\,j \\ &\quad {}+\sin{\left(t \right)}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(\tan{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(\sec{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(\sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ & =\left(4 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- \cos{\left(t \right)} \tan{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(\sin{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ & =2 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(2 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[- \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ & =\left(- \cos{\left(2 \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(- \cos{\left(2 \left(0\right) \right)}\right)\right) \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\left(1\right) \\ & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ given that $F(x,y,z)=\left(x\right)\,i+\left(z\right)\,j+\left(y\right)\,k$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=\left(\sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(\sec{\left(t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi}{3}]$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=\sin{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=\sec{\left(t \right)},\qquad z=3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+z\,j+y\,k \\ & =\left(\left(\sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(\sec{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,k \\ & =\sin{\left(t \right)}\,i+3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,j \\ &\quad {}+\sec{\left(t \right)}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\sec{\left(t \right)}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\,k \\ & =\cos{\left(t \right)}\,i \\ &\quad {}+\tan{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\,j \\ &\quad {}+- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(\sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(\cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(\tan{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(\sec{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ & =\left(\sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)} \tan{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} \sec{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ & =\frac{\sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(\frac{\sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[- \frac{\cos{\left(2 t \right)}}{4}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ & =\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(2 \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \right)}}{4}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(2 \left(0\right) \right)}}{4}\right)\right) \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $AC=9\,\text{mm}$. Checking the area gives $\frac12\cdot\left(11\right)\cdot\left(9\right)\cdot\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)=\frac{99 \sqrt{2}}{4}\,\text{mm}^2$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2$. The point $P(2,-3,5)$ lies on $C$, and

$$
f_y(x,y)=- y - 2
$$

Find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P$.

Use $m=f_y(2,-3)$ and $z-z_0=m(y-y_0)$, keeping $x=2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The plane fixes $x$, so $y$ varies along the section. Evaluate the supplied partial:

$$
\begin{aligned}m&=f_y(2,-3) \\ &=- \left(-3\right) - 2 \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form at $(y_0,z_0)=(-3,5)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-(5)&=(1)(y-(-3)) \\ z&=y + 8\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent retains the fixed-coordinate plane:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2 \\ z &=y + 8\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x&=2 \\ z-(-4)&=(1)(y-(-2))\end{aligned}\right.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2 & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\langle 0,-1,-1\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Negating this cross product gives $\langle 0,1,1\rangle$.

Any nonzero scalar multiple is valid. The listed answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}1\left(\langle 0,1,1\rangle\right) & =\langle 0,1,1\rangle\end{aligned}

It has the required component ratio $v_z/v_y=1$.

question.:question/problem:
![](circulation-dd8184004ce2245e58da.png)

Consider the ellipse and vector field $\mathbf F$ shown above. Let $C$ traverse the curve once in the **counterclockwise** direction. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $\Gamma=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r$ measures the work done around a *closed* curve. Assistance gives positive work, opposition gives negative work, and perpendicular force gives zero work.

The field opposes the motion all the way around $C$ in the **counterclockwise** direction.

![](circulation-76e8b525622c504f8f7d.png)

Thus, $\oint_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r < 0$. Reversing traversal reverses the work: $\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=-\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r$. The reversed path $-C$ is **clockwise**.

![](circulation-a469bf5a7c4c195a9613.png)

Therefore, $\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r > 0$.

- $\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r = 0$ is **false**.

- $\oint_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r < 0$ is **true**.

- $\oint_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r > 0$ is **false**.

Therefore, select $\oint_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r < 0$.

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Using a Substitution

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=- y$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2 t^{2},t\rangle,\qquad 1\le t\le \sqrt{2}.
$$

Give the exact value.

Use the scalar line integral formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm ds &=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(2 t^{2})\,i+(t)\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=2 t^{2}$, $y=t$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =(4 t)\,i+(1)\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(4 t)^2+(1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{16 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=- y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(-1)(t) \\  & =- t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}(- t)(\sqrt{16 t^{2} + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $f(x, y) = \cos x + 4x^{2}y$ increase most rapidly at the point $(2, 2)$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\cos x + 4x^{2}y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\cos x + 4x^{2}y)\,j \\ & =(-\sin x+8xy)\,i+(4x^{2})\,j \\ ∇f(2,2) & =(-\sin (2)+8\cdot (2)\cdot (2))\,i+(4\cdot (2)^{2})\,j \\ & =(32 -\sin{(2 )})\,i+16\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $(32 -\sin{(2 )})\,i+16\,j.$

$$
