question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral

$$
\int_C (x + y)\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle - 2 t, 1 - 2 t\rangle.
$$

The parameter interval is $1\leq t\leq 2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar line-integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates and compute the speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle -2, -2\rangle \\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-2)^2} \\
&=2 \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$



Substitute the coordinates into the density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(1)\left((- 2 t)+(1 - 2 t)\right) \\
&=1 - 4 t
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply by the speed and integrate, subtracting the lower endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{2} (1 - 4 t)\cdot (2 \sqrt{2})\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{1}^{2} - 8 \sqrt{2} t + 2 \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- 4 \sqrt{2} t^{2} + 2 \sqrt{2} t\right]_{1}^{2} \\
&=(- 12 \sqrt{2})-(- 2 \sqrt{2}) \\
&=- 10 \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the scalar line-integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.

Differentiate both coordinates and compute the speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}

&=\sqrt{9(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)}=3
\end{aligned}
$$

Use $2\cos^2t-1=\cos 2t$.

Substitute the coordinates into the density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(1)\left(2(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2-9\right) \\
&=(9)(2\cos^2t-1) \\

\end{aligned}

$$

&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} 27 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[\left(\frac{27}{2}\right)\sin 2t\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\
&=\left(\frac{27}{2}\right)-(0) \\
&=\frac{27}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the scalar line-integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates and compute the speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=(3)(-\sin t+\sin t+t\cos t)=3 t \cos{\left(t \right)} \\
y'(t)&=(3)(\cos t-\cos t+t\sin t)=3 t \sin{\left(t \right)} \\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{9t^2(\cos^2t+\sin^2t)} \\
&=3|t|=3 t
\end{aligned}
$$

The product-rule terms cancel in each derivative. On the supplied interval, $t\geq0$, so $|t|=t$. In the sum of squared coordinates, the two mixed terms cancel.

Substitute the coordinates into the density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(t)^2+y(t)^2&=9\bigl[(\cos t+t\sin t)^2 \\
&\qquad +(\sin t-t\cos t)^2\bigr] \\
&=9\bigl[\cos^2t+\sin^2t \\
&\qquad +t^2(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\bigr] \\
&=9(1+t^2) \\
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(9)(1+t^2)+(-1) \\
&=9 t^{2} + 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply by the speed and integrate, subtracting the lower endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{0}^{2} (9 t^{2} + 8)\cdot (3 t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{2} 27 t^{3} + 24 t\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[\frac{27 t^{4}}{4} + 12 t^{2}\right]_{0}^{2} \\
&=(156)-(0) \\
&=156
\end{aligned}
$$

&=3|t|=3 t
\end{aligned}
$$

The product-rule terms cancel in each derivative. On the supplied interval, $t\geq0$, so $|t|=t$. In the sum of squared coordinates, the two mixed terms cancel.

Substitute the coordinates into the density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(t)^2+y(t)^2&=9\bigl[(\cos t+t\sin t)^2 \\
&\qquad +(\sin t-t\cos t)^2\bigr] \\
&=9\bigl[\cos^2t+\sin^2t \\
&\qquad +t^2(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\bigr] \\
&=9(1+t^2) \\
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(-9)(1+t^2)+(-2) \\
&=- 9 t^{2} - 11
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{0}^{1} (- 9 t^{2} - 11)\cdot (3 t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\

&=\left[- \frac{27 t^{4}}{4} - \frac{33 t^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\
&=\left(- \frac{93}{4}\right)-(0) \\
&=- \frac{93}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left(- 2 x\right)\mathbf i+\left(- 2 y\right)\mathbf j
$$

along the closed curve $C$, traversed once according to

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\mathbf i+\left(3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\mathbf j,\qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Circulation is total work around the closed path:

$$
\Gamma=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r\prime(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Substitute the path into the field and differentiate the path:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))&=\left(- 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\mathbf i\\
&\quad+\left(- 6 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\mathbf j,\\
\mathbf r\prime(t)&=\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\mathbf i\\
&\quad+\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product of corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r\prime(t)\\
&=\left(- 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\\
&\quad+\left(- 6 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ and collecting terms gives

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r\prime(t)=0.
$$

Integrate over the complete traversal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(0\right)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[0\right]_0^{2\pi}\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The dot product is constant on this path.

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate ${\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(- 2 y + 1)\,i+(- 2 x - 1)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(- 2 t + 1)\,i+(- t + 2)\,j$ for $t\in[0,1].$

*Hint:* Use $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- 2 t + 1,\quad y=- t + 2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(- 2 y + 1)\,i+(- 2 x - 1)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(- 2 \left(- t + 2\right) + 1\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(- 2 t + 1\right) - 1\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(2 t - 3)\,i+(4 t - 3)\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t + 1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t + 2)\,j \\  & =(-2)\,i+(-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(2 t - 3)\,i+(4 t - 3)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(-2)\,i+(-1)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=(2 t - 3)\cdot(-2)+(4 t - 3)\cdot(-1) \\ &=\left({- 4 t + 6}\right)+\left({- 4 t + 3}\right) \\ &=- 8 t + 9\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({- 8 t + 9}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- 4 t^{2} + 9 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((-4)+(9))-((0)+(0)) \\ &=(5)-(0) \\ &=5\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

*Hint:* Use $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- 2 t - 1,\quad y=- 2 t - 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(- 2 y - 2)\,i+(- 2 x + y - 1)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(- 2 \left(- 2 t - 1\right) - 2\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(- 2 t - 1\right) + \left(- 2 t - 1\right) - 1\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(4 t)\,i+(2 t)\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t - 1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t - 1)\,j \\  & =(-2)\,i+(-2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(4 t)\,i+(2 t)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(-2)\,i+(-2)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=(4 t)\cdot(-2)+(2 t)\cdot(-2) \\ &=\left({- 8 t}\right)+\left({- 4 t}\right) \\ &=- 12 t\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({- 12 t}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- 6 t^{2}}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((-6))-((0)) \\ &=(-6)-(0) \\ &=-6\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate ${\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(- y - 2)\,i+(- x - 2)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(t + 2)\,i+(2 t + 1)\,j$ for $t\in[0,1].$

*Hint:* Use $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t + 2,\quad y=2 t + 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(- y - 2)\,i+(- x - 2)\,j \\ &=\left(- \left(2 t + 1\right) - 2\right)\,i+\left(- \left(t + 2\right) - 2\right)\,j \\ &=(- 2 t - 3)\,i+(- t - 4)\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t + 2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 1)\,j \\  & =(1)\,i+(2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(- 2 t - 3)\,i+(- t - 4)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(1)\,i+(2)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 2 t - 3)\cdot(1)+(- t - 4)\cdot(2) \\ &=\left({- 2 t - 3}\right)+\left({- 2 t - 8}\right) \\ &=- 4 t - 11\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({- 4 t - 11}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- 2 t^{2} - 11 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((-11)+(-2))-((0)+(0)) \\ &=(-13)-(0) \\ &=-13\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\quad y=t + 2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(- 2 x^{2} y)\,i+(- 2 x - 2)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(- 2 \left(t\right)^{2} \left(t + 2\right)\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(t\right) - 2\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(2 t^{2} \left(- t - 2\right))\,i+(- 2 t - 2)\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t + 2)\,j \\  & =(1)\,i+(1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(2 t^{2} \left(- t - 2\right))\,i+(- 2 t - 2)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(1)\,i+(1)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 t^{2} \left(- t - 2\right))\cdot(1)+(- 2 t - 2) \\ &{} \cdot(1)\end{aligned} \\ &=\left({- 2 t^{3} - 4 t^{2}}\right)+\left({- 2 t - 2}\right) \\ &=- 2 t^{3} - 4 t^{2} - 2 t - 2\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{1}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{2}\left({- 2 t^{3} - 4 t^{2} - 2 t - 2}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- \frac{t^{4}}{2} - \frac{4 t^{3}}{3} - t^{2} - 2 t}\right]_{1}^{2} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&((-4)+(-4)+\left(- \frac{32}{3}\right)+(-8)) \\ &{} -((-1)+(-2)+\left(- \frac{4}{3}\right)+\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right))\end{aligned} \\ &=\left(- \frac{80}{3}\right)-\left(- \frac{29}{6}\right) \\ &=- \frac{131}{6}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(2 y)\,i+(- 2 x)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(2 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j$ for $t\in[\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3 \pi}{2}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2 \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad y=3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(2 y)\,i+(- 2 x)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(2 \left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(6 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(2 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(6 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(2 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(6 \cos{\left(t \right)})\cdot(2 \cos{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)})\cdot(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\left({12 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}}\right)+\left({12 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}\right) \\ &=12\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\left({12}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{12 t}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}} \\ &=((18 \pi))-((6 \pi)) \\ &=(18 \pi)-(6 \pi) \\ &=12 \pi\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3 \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad y=\cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(2 y)\,i+(- 2 x)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(2 \left(\cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(2 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 6 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(2 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 6 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 \cos{\left(t \right)})\cdot(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(- 6 \sin{\left(t \right)})\cdot(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\left({6 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}}\right)+\left({6 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}\right) \\ &=6\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{\pi}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{\pi}\left({6}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{6 t}\right]_{0}^{\pi} \\ &=((6 \pi))-((0)) \\ &=(6 \pi)-(0) \\ &=6 \pi\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(2 x + 1)\,i+(2 y + 1)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j$ for $t\in[0,\frac{3 \pi}{2}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad y=t \cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(2 x + 1)\,i+(2 y + 1)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(2 \left(t \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) + 1\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(2 \left(t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) + 1\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,i \\ &{} +(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,i \\ &{} +(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,j\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1) \\ &{} \cdot(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 1) \\ &{} \cdot(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + 2 t \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} +\left({\begin{aligned}&- 2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} - t \sin{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + 2 t \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\left({\begin{aligned}&- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{t^{2} + t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)}}\right]_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(\left(\frac{9 \pi^{2}}{4}\right)+(0)+\left(- \frac{3 \pi}{2}\right)) \\ &{} -((0)+(0)+(0))\end{aligned} \\ &=(- \frac{3 \pi}{2} + \frac{9 \pi^{2}}{4})-(0) \\ &=\frac{3 \pi \left(-2 + 3 \pi\right)}{4}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

The offset terms integrate by the reverse product rule:

$$
\begin{gathered}\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(t^{2} + t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(- 2 x + 2)\,i+(- 2 y - 2)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(- 2 \left(t \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) + 2\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) - 2\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2)\,i \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2)\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2)\,i \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2)\,j\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2) \\ &{} \cdot(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2) \\ &{} \cdot(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&- 2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} +\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- t^{2} + 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)}}\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&((- 4 \pi^{2})+(- 4 \pi)+(0)) \\ &{} -((0)+(0)+(0))\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 4 \pi^{2} - 4 \pi)-(0) \\ &=- 4 \pi \left(1 + \pi\right)\end{aligned}\end{gathered}

$$

\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1)\,i \\ &{} +(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,j\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({\begin{aligned}&(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1) \\ &{} \cdot(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1) \\ &{} \cdot(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} + t \sin{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} +\left({\begin{aligned}&- 2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\left({\begin{aligned}&t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- t^{2} + t \sin{\left(t \right)} - t \cos{\left(t \right)}}\right]_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(\left(- \frac{9 \pi^{2}}{4}\right)+\left(- \frac{3 \pi}{2}\right)+(0)) \\ &{} -((0)+(0)+(0))\end{aligned} \\ &=(- \frac{9 \pi^{2}}{4} - \frac{3 \pi}{2})-(0) \\ &=- \frac{3 \pi \left(2 + 3 \pi\right)}{4}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

The offset terms integrate by the reverse product rule:

$$
\begin{gathered}\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- t^{2} + t \sin{\left(t \right)} - t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the general form of $f(x,y)$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f={}&\bigl(- y - 3\bigr)\,\mathbf i\\
&+\bigl(- x - 2\bigr)\,\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$

Work on $\mathbb R^2$.

In the choices, $C$ is an arbitrary constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector components are $f_x$ and $f_y$. Integrate the first component with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as constant. Retain an arbitrary function $g(y)$ because its $x$-derivative is zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=\int\bigl(- y - 3\bigr)\,\mathrm dx\\
&=- x y - 3 x+g(y).
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate with respect to $y$ and match the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y&=- x+g'(y)\\
g'(y)&=\bigl(- x - 2\bigr)\\
&\quad-\bigl(- x\bigr)\\
&=-2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate the remaining function of $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(y)&=\int\bigl(-2\bigr)\,\mathrm dy\\
&=- 2 y+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute to obtain

$$
f(x,y)=- x y - 3 x - 2 y+C
$$

Both components check:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x&=- y - 3,\\
f_y&=- x - 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,z)&=\left(2 y\right)\,\mathbf{i} \\ &{}+\left(2 x\right)\,\mathbf{j} \\ &{}+\left(1\right)\,\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathbf{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=2 y \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=2 x \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=1\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=2 x y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=2 x \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(0\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=2 x y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=h'(z).
$$

Comparing this derivative with the third component and subtracting the known terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}h'(z)&=1 \\ h(z)&=z+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=2 x y + z+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathbf{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=- 6 x y \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=- 3 x^{2} + 4 y z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=2 y^{2} - 2 z\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(- 6 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=- 3 x^{2} y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=- 3 x^{2}+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=- 3 x^{2} + 4 y z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}- 3 x^{2}+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=- 3 x^{2} + 4 y z \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=4 y z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(4 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=2 y^{2} z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=2 y^{2} z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=- 3 x^{2} y + 2 y^{2} z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=2 y^{2}+h'(z).
$$

Comparing this derivative with the third component and subtracting the known terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}h'(z)&=- 2 z \\ h(z)&=- z^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=- 3 x^{2} y + 2 y^{2} z - z^{2}+C.
$$

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathbf{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=2 y z e^{x z} + z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=2 e^{x z} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=2 x y e^{x z} + x + 2 z\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(2 y z e^{x z} + z\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=x z + 2 y e^{x z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 e^{x z}+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 e^{x z}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 e^{x z}+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=2 e^{x z} \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(0\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x z + 2 y e^{x z}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=2 x y e^{x z} + x+h'(z).
$$

Comparing this derivative with the third component and subtracting the known terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}h'(z)&=2 z \\ h(z)&=z^{2}+C\end{aligned}

where $C$ is a constant.

$$
f(x,y,z)=x z + 2 y e^{x z} + z^{2}+C.

$$

$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 e^{x z} + 1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 e^{x z}+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=2 e^{x z} + 1 \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=1\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathbf{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=- 2 x z + 3 \sin{\left(y \right)} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=3 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 6 z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=- x^{2} + 6 y + 4 z\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(- 2 x z + 3 \sin{\left(y \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=- x^{2} z + 3 x \sin{\left(y \right)}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=3 x \cos{\left(y \right)}+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=3 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 6 z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3 x \cos{\left(y \right)}+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=3 x \cos{\left(y \right)} + 6 z \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=6 z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(6 z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=6 y z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=6 y z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=- x^{2} z + 3 x \sin{\left(y \right)} + 6 y z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=- x^{2} + 6 y+h'(z).
$$

Comparing this derivative with the third component and subtracting the known terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}h'(z)&=4 z \\ h(z)&=2 z^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

$$
f(x,y,z)=- x^{2} z + 3 x \sin{\left(y \right)} + 6 y z + 2 z^{2}+C.

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{v}=\left\langle -5,2\right\rangle$. Find its exact magnitude. Use $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The components are $v_x=-5$ and $v_y=2$. Square each entire signed component, then add.

$$
\begin{aligned}
|\mathbf{v}|&=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\\
&=\sqrt{\left(-5\right)^2+\left(2\right)^2}\\
&=\sqrt{25+4}\\
&=\sqrt{29}\\
&= \sqrt{29}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude is nonnegative.

Squaring the first component twice introduces a fourth power; square each component once.
The formula adds the component squares; it does not subtract them.
Correct: square both components, add, and take the nonnegative square root.
Adding signed components does not give the Euclidean length.

Both radicands must be nonnegative. The complete shifted denominator must also be nonzero.

$$
\begin{aligned}

x^2+y^2-9&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^2+y^2\ge9\\

The right side of the root equation is positive, so squaring is reversible. Exclude this level set. The radicand-zero boundary remains allowed wherever the numerator is real, since the denominator there is $-1$.

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,\begin{aligned}y &\le0\\x^2+y^2 &\ge9\\x^2+y^2 &\ne10\end{aligned}\right\}.

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,\begin{aligned}x-y &\le0\\x^2+y^2 &\le4\\x^2+y^2 &\ne3\end{aligned}\right\}.

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector

question.:question/problem: Let $n=\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}$. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $n$ and points the same direction.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector and points the same direction, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
\begin{aligned}u &= \frac{n}{|n|}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|n| &= \sqrt{(-8)^2+(-6)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{100} \\
&= 10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $n$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u &= \frac{n}{|n|} \\
&= \frac{1}{10}\cdot (n) \\
&= \frac{1}{10}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}- \frac{4}{5} \\ - \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=2^{\frac{y^{2}}{x+1}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The inner quotient requires $x+1\ne 0$. The outer function is defined for every real input and adds no further restriction.

Intersecting these conditions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\,x+1\ne 0\}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\ln\left(4-y^{2}\right)}{x+2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The logarithm requires $4-y^{2}>0$.

The denominator must be nonzero, so $x+2\ne 0$.

Intersecting these conditions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4-y^{2}>0 \\ x+2\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\,\begin{aligned}&4-y^{2}>0 \\ &x+2\ne 0\end{aligned}\right\}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\ln\left(x+2y+2\right)}{e^{y-1}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The logarithm requires $x+2y+2>0$.

The denominator $e^{y-1}$ is positive for every real input, so it never vanishes.

Intersecting these conditions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y+2>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\,x+2y+2>0\}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{\ln\left(-x^{3}y\right)}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The logarithm requires $-x^{3}y>0$. Its value is a denominator, so it must also be nonzero.

On positive inputs, $\ln\left(-x^{3}y\right)=0$ exactly when $-x^{3}y=1$. Thus we must exclude $-x^{3}y=1$, even when the numerator is zero.

Intersecting these conditions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-x^{3}y>0 \\ -x^{3}y\ne 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\,\begin{aligned}&-x^{3}y>0 \\ &-x^{3}y\ne 1\end{aligned}\right\}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\arccos\left(y+\sqrt{x-1}\right).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The inner square root requires $x-1\ge 0$.

The input of $\arccos$ must lie in the closed interval $[-1,1]$, including both endpoints. Therefore $-1\le y+\sqrt{x-1}\le 1$.

Intersecting these conditions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1\le y+\sqrt{x-1}\le 1 \\ x-1\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\,\begin{aligned}&-1\le y+\sqrt{x-1}\le 1 \\ &x-1\ge 0\end{aligned}\right\}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The inner quotient requires $x+y+1\ne 0$.

The input of $\arcsin$ must lie in the closed interval $[-1,1]$, including both endpoints. Therefore $-1\le \frac{1}{x+y+1}\le 1$.

Intersecting these conditions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1\le \frac{1}{x+y+1}\le 1 \\ x+y+1\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\,\begin{aligned}&-1\le \frac{1}{x+y+1}\le 1 \\ &x+y+1\ne 0\end{aligned}\right\}.
$$

Let $A(0,3)$ and $B(4,1)$. Find $|\overset{\to }{AB}|$. Do not round the answer.

$|\overset{\to }{AB}|=$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=3 j, \\ & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=4 i + j.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} &= \overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\ &= b-a \\ &= (4 i + j)-(3 j) \\ &= 4 i - 2 j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{AB}| &= \sqrt{(4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\ &= \sqrt{16+4} \\ &= \sqrt{20} \\ &= 2 \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2&=\left(- 4 e^{2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + 8 e^{2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(8 e^{2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + 4 e^{2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &=16e^{4t}(2\cos t-\sin t)^2 \\ &\quad+16e^{4t}(2\sin t+\cos t)^2 \\ &=80e^{4t}(\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t) \\ &=80 e^{4 t}\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Expressing a Line Integral as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the boundary of the unit square, traversed counterclockwise, and let $D$ be its interior.

Use Green's theorem to choose the function $f(x,y)$ in

$$
\begin{aligned}&\oint_C\left(- 2 y^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\\&\quad+\left(x^{2} + x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The stated traversal is **counterclockwise**. Green's theorem applies because both coefficients have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$. For this orientation,

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

![The region and oriented boundary.](images/aa/aa60dd35a920d166f7cc3238a366bde93bd2c33e1b39b0a38313ab46a8de2d8b.png)

Identify the coefficients of the two differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y)&=- 2 y^{2},\\Q(x,y)&=x^{2} + x y.\end{aligned}
$$

Hold the other variable constant when taking each partial derivative. Apply the power rule to each relevant term.

$$
\begin{aligned}P_y&=- 4 y,\\Q_x&=2 x + y.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtract the entire derivative in the order required by the traversal, then collect like terms:

$$

question.:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate

$$
\oint_C \left(- x^{2} - 2 y + 1\right)\,dx+\left(x - y^{2} + 1\right)\,dy
$$

where $C$ is the boundary of the rectangle $-2\le x\le 0$, $1\le y\le 4$, traversed counterclockwise.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve. The components have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, so

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,dA.
$$

Here $P=- x^{2} - 2 y + 1$ and $Q=x - y^{2} + 1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=-2,\\
Q_x&=1,\\
Q_x-P_y&=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The supplied rectangular bounds give independent limits.

$$
D=\{(x,y):-2\le x\le 0,\ 1\le y\le 4\}.
$$

The shaded region and counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](region-b260a20b6a18bde40848.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy&=\int_{-2}^{0}\int_{1}^{4}\left(3\right)\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_{-2}^{0}\left[3 y\right]_{1}^{4}\,dx\\
&=\int_{-2}^{0}\left(9\right)\,dx\\
&=\left[9 x\right]_{-2}^{0}\\
&=0-\left(-18\right)\\
&=18.
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearrange and divide by the positive constant $36$ to obtain $\frac{x^{2}}{4} + \frac{y^{2}}{9}<1$. The boundary is centered at $(0,0)$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $3$. Shade **inside** it. The boundary is **excluded** (dashed).

$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the real-valued function $f(x,y)=\frac{3}{\ln\!\left(- \frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{2} + 1\right)}$?

The logarithm needs a positive argument, and its value in the denominator must be nonzero.

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{2} + 1&>0 \\ \ln\!\left(- \frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{2} + 1\right)&\ne0 \\ - \frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{2} + 1&\ne1 \\ - x - y + 2&\ne 2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\ln(1)=0$ and the logarithm is one-to-one on positive inputs, its argument must differ from $1$. Multiplying both restrictions by the positive constant $2$ gives $- x - y + 2>0,\quad - x - y + 2\ne 2$. Shade the half-plane $- x - y + 2>0$ and remove the parallel line $- x - y + 2=2$. Both lines are **excluded**, so draw them dashed. Keep both portions of the positive half-plane separated by the removed line.

Therefore,

$$
D=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\;:\;\begin{aligned}- x - y + 2&>0 \\ - x - y + 2&\ne 2\end{aligned}\right\}.
$$
